qs.q: Which artery is a direct branch of the femoral artery, typically arising proximally in the femoral triangle?
qs.e: The profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery is the largest branch of the femoral artery, typically arising about 3.5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Perforating arteries are branches of the profunda femoris artery. The obturator and inferior epigastric arteries are branches of the internal and external iliac arteries, respectively.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Anatomy Exam - May 22, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The femoral triangle is a superficial compartment in the upper thigh that contains the femoral nerve, artery, vein and lymphatics. It is bounded by the inguinal ligament, sartorius, and adductor longus, and is a key site for vascular access and for recognizing thigh pathology.

sections.p: A shallow, inverted triangular space in the anterior thigh that provides easy access to the femoral vessels and nerve, making it clinically important for procedures and trauma assessment.
b: Boundaries: inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial)
Floor: iliopsoas tendon, pectineus, and fascia lata

sections.p: Located just below the inguinal ligament, the triangle lies between the sartorius and adductor longus muscles. Its apex points toward the adductor hiatus.
b: Apex at the adductor hiatus where the femoral vessels pass into the popliteal fossa
Base formed by the inguinal ligament

sections.p: From lateral to medial the contents are remembered by the mnemonic NAVEL: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty (deep femoral vein), Lymphatics.
b: Femoral nerve lies most lateral, then artery, then vein, then deep femoral vein, then lymphatics
Great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein just inferior to the inguinal ligament

sections.p: The femoral artery, a continuation of the external iliac artery, supplies the lower limb and gives off the profunda femoris (deep femoral) branch within the triangle.
b: Femoral artery is palpable just below the inguinal ligament
Profunda femoris supplies thigh muscles and anastomoses with the popliteal artery

t.b: Is there arterial occlusion or aneurysm? A dampened signal suggests stenosis; a pulsatile mass suggests aneurysm
Is peripheral arterial disease present? <0.9 indicates disease; normal >0.9

sections.p: The femoral nerve, derived from L2‑L4, lies lateral in the triangle and provides motor innervation to the anterior thigh muscles and sensory supply to the anterior thigh and medial leg.
b: Branches: anterior cutaneous nerves, saphenous nerve (sensory)

t.a: Nerve conduction study of femoral nerve
t.b: Is there neuropathy? Reduced amplitude indicates axonal loss; prolonged latency suggests demyelination

sections.p: Allows passage of neurovascular structures to the lower limb and provides a superficial window for clinical examination, catheterisation, and emergency control of bleeding.
b: Site for femoral artery cannulation in shock
Compression point for controlling femoral hemorrhage

sections.p: Injury or disease affecting the triangle can compromise limb perfusion, cause nerve palsy, or lead to life‑threatening bleeding. Common problems include femoral hernia, vascular trauma, and deep vein thrombosis.
b: Femoral hernia protrudes through the femoral canal, more common in women
Traumatic femoral artery injury → rapid exsanguination; requires immediate pressure
Deep femoral vein thrombosis may present with swelling and pain

t.b: If ultrasound unavailable, use clinical Wells score and treat empirically in high‑risk settings
Is there arterial injury or aneurysm? Contrast extravasation indicates active bleed

sections.p: Physical exam of the femoral triangle provides quick clues to vascular and neural integrity.
b: Palpate femoral pulse just inferior to inguinal ligament; absent pulse suggests arterial occlusion
Test saphenous nerve sensation on medial leg; loss indicates nerve injury
Assess quadriceps strength (knee extension) for femoral nerve function

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of femoral pulse with leg pain (possible arterial occlusion)
Rapidly expanding groin mass with pain (possible femoral artery aneurysm or hemorrhage)
Severe groin pain after trauma with swelling (possible femoral vein injury)

faq.q: Why is the femoral triangle important for emergency access?
faq.a: It provides a superficial, compressible site to insert catheters or apply pressure to control bleeding.

faq.q: What is the most common hernia in the femoral triangle?
faq.a: Femoral hernia, especially in women, protrudes through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament.

faq.q: How can I differentiate femoral from inguinal hernia clinically?
faq.a: Femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament and are more lateral; inguinal hernias are above the ligament.

exam: Describe the boundaries and contents of the femoral triangle using the NAVEL mnemonic.
Explain how you would control a femoral artery bleed in a low‑resource setting.
Identify the clinical signs of femoral nerve injury and their anatomical basis.
